title: A case-control study on the characteristics and treatment regimens of type 2 diabetes mellitus in HIV-positive patients compared with HIV-negative patients with diabetes
summary:
Background:
Thanks to modern treatment, people with HIV now live significantly longer. As a result, other health conditions are increasingly occurring alongside HIV infection. These include, among others, obesity, metabolic disorders, and type 2 diabetes (“adult-onset diabetes”).
In addition to the usual risk factors, other factors may play a role in people with HIV. These include: chronic activation of the immune system, other infections, and changes in body weight due to modern HIV therapy. Earlier therapies also had an adverse effect on metabolism. Studies have described greater weight gain, particularly with integrase inhibitors and tenofovir.
Research is underway to determine whether there is a possible link between taking integrase inhibitors and the risk of diabetes.
For people with HIV, there are recommendations—known as guidelines—on how to diagnose and treat metabolic disorders and diabetes. However, these recommendations do not differ fundamentally from those for people without HIV. In treatment, however, potential drug interactions, the specific characteristics of HIV therapy, and kidney function should be taken into account.

Research Question/Objective of the Study:
There has been insufficient research into whether people with HIV and type 2 diabetes mellitus differ from patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus who do not have HIV.
The objective of this study is therefore to compare the medical data of these groups in order to identify any possible differences.

Methodology:
Only data collected as part of routine medical care and fully recorded in the respective medical records by August 24, 2026, at the latest, will be used. For both groups, the following data are recorded from routine documentation: age, sex, height, weight, BMI, country or region of origin, smoking status, blood pressure, date or year of initial diabetes diagnosis, current diabetes treatment, relevant comorbidities, and concomitant medications. In addition, laboratory parameters relevant to diabetes, kidney function, and HIV infection will be recorded approximately 3–6 months before the so-called index date, August 24, 2026.
conditions: Asymptomatic human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] infection status
